title: Zophar: God Exacts Less Than You Deserve
summary: Zophar, the third friend, speaks for the first time and is the harshest yet. He accuses Job of empty talk, wishes God would speak and show Job the secrets of wisdom, and tells him that God is actually punishing him less than his sin deserves. God's depths are beyond knowing, he says, but if Job turns his heart to God and puts away his sin, his life will be brighter than noonday.
story: The first round of speeches is nearly complete. Eliphaz spoke gently of God's discipline (chapters 4 and 5); Bildad appealed to tradition and implied that Job's children died for their sins (chapter 8). Job has answered each of them and, in chapters 9 and 10, poured out his case directly to God. Now Zophar speaks, and his tone is the most impatient. He does something the others only hinted at: he flatly tells Job that he is guilty. Ironically, Zophar wishes that God would speak and set Job straight (verse 5). Much later, God does speak (chapters 38 to 41), but his rebuke falls on the friends as well as on Job (42:7).
historical:
Zophar is called the Naamathite, from a place called Naamah. A town with that name appears in Judah's territory (Joshua 15:41), but since Job's friends come from the peoples to the east, most interpreters think Zophar's home was somewhere in the region of Edom or northern Arabia. Its exact location is unknown. As with the other friends, the book shows a man outside Israel who knows the one God and speaks confidently about him.

Zophar's words reflect a view of divine justice widespread in the ancient world: gods rewarded the faithful and punished the wicked in this life, and misfortune was the sign that some offense had been committed, perhaps unknowingly. Mesopotamian prayers sometimes ask a god to reveal an unknown sin so the sufferer can confess it. Zophar goes further by assuming he already knows the answer: Job's suffering proves his guilt, even if no one can name the sin.
cultural:
When Zophar tells Job to lift up his hands to God (verse 13), he describes a common posture of prayer in Israel and the ancient Near East. The one praying stood and spread open palms toward heaven, a gesture of appeal and of empty-handedness before God. Putting away iniquity from the hand (verse 14) plays on that picture: hands raised in prayer should be clean.

The proverb in verse 12, about a witless man and a wild donkey's colt, sounds like a folk saying. The wild donkey was proverbial in the ancient Near East for being untamed and stubborn (Genesis 16:12 uses it of Ishmael). Zophar's point is insulting: a man as foolish as Job is as likely to become wise as a wild donkey is to be born human. Ancient wisdom debate could be sharp and personal, and Zophar's sarcasm is meant to sting.
literary: Zophar's speech has three movements. Verses 2-6 rebuke Job, quoting his claim to be pure and wishing God would reveal the hidden side of wisdom. Verses 7-12 are a short hymn to God's unsearchable depths, measured by the four directions of the cosmos: higher than the heavens, deeper than Sheol, longer than the earth, wider than the sea. Verses 13-20 are a call to repentance with a promise of restoration, closing with a warning about the wicked. The structure resembles the endings of Eliphaz's and Bildad's speeches, which also close with a picture of the restored penitent. Zophar's hymn to the unsearchable God in verses 7-9 is some of the most beautiful poetry in the friends' speeches, and it anticipates themes God himself will raise in chapter 38, which makes it all the more ironic that Zophar uses it to claim certainty about Job's guilt.

outline.t: Zophar rebukes Job and wishes God would speak
Repent and your life will be bright again

doctrines.note: Zophar rightly confesses that God's wisdom is beyond human measure, higher than heaven and deeper than Sheol. The irony is that he claims to know exactly what God is doing in Job's life while insisting no one can fathom God.
Zophar's call to turn the heart, lift the hands, and put away sin is a sound description of repentance. It becomes cruel because he assumes Job's suffering is proof of hidden guilt.

Verse 6 speaks of the secrets of wisdom and says true wisdom has two sides, meaning there is more to it than appears. The book agrees and will show that the hidden side of Job's story is one Zophar himself cannot see.

words.note: Cheqer, searching or what is found by searching. Verse 7 asks whether Job can find out the searching of God, that is, reach the bottom of his depths. The same word appeared in Bildad's appeal to the findings of the fathers (8:8) and in Job's praise of God's unsearchable works (9:10).

Tushiyyah, sound wisdom or effective insight, a word found mostly in Job and Proverbs. In verse 6 Zophar speaks of wisdom that has two sides or is double. The phrase is difficult; it likely means that real wisdom has a hidden dimension beyond what is visible.

Tiqvah, hope, from a root meaning to wait or to stretch toward something (it can also mean a cord). Zophar promises Job security because there is hope (verse 18), then ends with the wicked, whose hope is only their last breath (verse 20).

Avon, iniquity or the guilt that comes from it. In verse 6 Zophar says God has overlooked some of Job's guilt. The word can mean the wrong itself, the guilt it creates, or its punishment, and Zophar's use assumes all three are present in Job's case.

christ: Zophar's hymn to God's unsearchable depths (verses 7-9) has a close cousin in the New Testament. After tracing God's plan for Jews and Gentiles, Paul breaks into praise for the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God, whose judgments are unsearchable (Romans 11:33), and in Romans 11:35 he quotes a line from later in Job (41:11). The difference is instructive. Paul confesses God's hiddenness in wonder, while Zophar uses it to silence a sufferer. The New Testament also says that the hidden wisdom of God has been revealed in Christ crucified (1 Corinthians 1:23-24; 2:7), which is the deepest reason Zophar's confident reading of suffering fails. In the cross, the one who suffered most was the one who had done no wrong.

hard.q: Is Zophar right that God gives us less than our sins deserve?
hard.a: In verse 6 Zophar says: “Know then that God exacts from you less than your iniquity deserves.” As a general statement, many biblical writers would agree that God does not treat people as their sins deserve (Psalm 103:10), and Christian theology holds that all have sinned and that every good gift is mercy. So the sentence contains a true idea. What makes it false here is its use. Zophar says it to a man whom God has called blameless, as an explanation for his losses, which means he is accusing Job of hidden sins worse than even his suffering. The book shows that this is exactly wrong: Job's suffering has a cause Zophar knows nothing about (chapters 1 and 2), and God later rebukes the friends (42:7). The lesson many readers draw is that a true doctrine can be spoken in a false way, and that speaking it to a sufferer as a verdict on his life is a failure of both truth and love.

questions: Zophar says God is beyond searching out, and in the same breath claims to know exactly why Job suffers. Where do you see that contradiction in yourself or others?
Zophar's promise of a brighter life if Job repents sounds hopeful. Why might it still be hurtful to someone in Job's position?
When is it right to tell a suffering friend they need to repent, and when is it wrong? What would help you tell the difference?
